headline: State desk: Pennsylvania legalization not a top priority, Costa says
dek: Pennsylvania's likely Senate leader put legalization behind other issues; Virginia weighs cannabis taxes for schools; Oklahoma gets a worker-safety grant.
key_points: Jay Costa, the presumptive president pro tempore of Pennsylvania's Senate, said legalization will be discussed but is not one of the high-priority items for the new Democratic majority.
Virginia lawmakers are weighing whether future cannabis tax revenue should pay for substance-use screening and counselling in schools, after a survey found 13% of secondary schools screen students.
A University of Oklahoma researcher has a CDC/NIOSH award to study exposures and health risks among Oklahoma cannabis workers.
All three items are about what states do with a legal market, or the prospect of one, after the 3 November elections.
body: Three state stories this week show the distance between winning an election and changing cannabis law. In Pennsylvania, the Democrat expected to lead the state Senate says adult-use legalization is not near the top of his list. In Virginia, lawmakers are already debating how to spend tax money from a retail market that does not yet exist. In Oklahoma, federal research money is going to the health of people who work in one of the country's largest medical markets.
## Pennsylvania: 'not necessarily right away'

Pennsylvania was the state where the midterms seemed to change the most for cannabis. As we reported after the election, Democrats won the state Senate, giving the party the governor's office and both chambers. Cannabis Business Times puts the new Senate majority at 26 to 24 after four seats flipped, the party's first Senate majority in 34 years.

Jay Costa, the Allegheny County Democrat who is the presumptive Senate president pro tempore, has now lowered expectations on timing. Speaking on abc27's This Week in Pennsylvania, in an interview published on 15 November, he said legalization would be looked at but "not necessarily right away" once Democrats take control in January.

Costa listed what he sees as coming first: affordability, a higher minimum wage, codifying reproductive rights, the statute of limitations for survivors of sexual abuse, housing and guardrails for AI data centres. He also named mass transit and transportation as matters to settle before the 1 July budget deadline. On cannabis, he said it is not one of the high-priority items the party feels it has been given a clear mandate to address, though he expects lawmakers to talk about it.

That sits awkwardly with other Democratic leaders. House Speaker Joanna McClinton said in September that if the party won both chambers it would move quickly on legalization, expungement and an equitable adult-use industry, Ganjapreneur notes. Gov. Josh Shapiro supports legalization and has counted cannabis tax revenue in several budget proposals. A March 2026 survey by Susquehanna Polling & Research found 69% of Pennsylvania voters in favour of regulating and taxing cannabis for adults, according to Cannabis Business Times.

The numbers explain some of the caution. A 26 to 24 majority means two Democratic defections would sink a bill unless Republicans cross over. The outgoing Senate voted 27 to 23 against a legalization framework, SB 49, on 10 June 2026. The budget deadline Costa mentioned is also the natural vehicle: Shapiro's budgets have assumed cannabis revenue, so the question may be settled in budget talks rather than as a stand-alone bill.

For operators, the timing matters more than the principle. As we reported earlier this month, six multi-state operators run 110 of Pennsylvania's 201 medical dispensaries. A legalization law in mid-2027 and one in 2028 are different propositions for anyone holding those licences. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire are the only two states in the Northeast without adult-use legalization, abc27 notes.
> Pennsylvania Democrats now have the votes on paper. What they do not yet have is agreement on when to use them.
## Virginia: spending the tax before the stores open

Virginia lawmakers are considering whether future cannabis tax revenue should fund substance-use prevention and counselling in public schools, Ganjapreneur reports, citing the Virginia Mercury. The discussion took place at the Joint Commission to Oversee the Transition of the Commonwealth into a Cannabis Retail Market.

The case rests on a September survey of schools presented by John Barfield, a policy analyst for the state's Behavioral Health Commission. It found that 13% of secondary schools use formal screening to identify students at risk of substance abuse, and about one in five have a substance-use counsellor. About 60% of the secondary schools that responded had a partnership with an outpatient provider, and about a third brought clinicians into school. Only 11% of elementary schools and 29% of secondary schools combined classroom teaching with evidence-based prevention programmes and community partnerships.
Barfield told the Mercury that schools worry about finding problems they lack the resources to treat. Screening without services, in other words, creates a liability.

Other states already earmark cannabis money this way. Citing the National Conference of State Legislatures, Ganjapreneur lists Illinois at 20% of cannabis tax revenue for mental health and substance-abuse programmes, Ohio at 25% for a substance abuse and addiction fund, New York at 20% of remaining revenue for drug treatment and public education, and Maine at 12% for a public health and safety fund, among others.

The size of the pot is the open question. As we reported, a state report estimated Virginia's cannabis market at $1.05 billion a year. Every earmark agreed now is a claim on revenue from that market before a single licensed sale. We covered the same commission's other proposals for the 2027 session on 17 November.
## Oklahoma: federal money for worker safety

Hongwan Li, an assistant professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Oklahoma's Hudson College of Public Health, has received a research award from the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health to study exposures and health risks among Oklahoma cannabis workers. The university announced the award on 2 November.

It is an R21 award, a federal grant type used for exploratory research, and it builds on the team's earlier pilot study. The university says the project will examine occupational exposures and identify ways to protect employees. Ganjapreneur reports that the pilot looked at respiratory hazards, including elevated carbon dioxide from plant respiration and particulate matter from tasks such as trimming and manufacturing.

The grant matters beyond Oklahoma because workplace exposure limits specific to cannabis cultivation and processing are thin. Findings from a federally funded study in a market with thousands of licensed businesses could shape guidance elsewhere. We covered related worker-safety research on 15 November. The award amount and study timeline were not given in the university's announcement.
## What to watch

In Pennsylvania, watch the Senate leadership vote and committee chairs when the new session opens in January, Shapiro's 2027 budget proposal, and the 1 July budget deadline. In Virginia, watch whether the joint commission writes a school funding share into its retail market bill for the 2027 session. In Oklahoma, watch for the study's first published exposure data.
